headline: Bangladesh achieves historic Test win against Australia on their own turf, marking a new era
summary: After years of struggle, Bangladesh's Test team secured an unforgettable victory against Australia in Darwin, showcasing a significant transformation in their approach and performance, especially with a potent pace attack.
details: Captain Najmul Hossain Shanto's pre-match conviction that 'The Bangladesh of 23 years ago and this Bangladesh are not the same' was met with skepticism, especially after a humiliating innings defeat against Zimbabwe and a low-scoring warm-up match.

However, by the fourth day of the Darwin Test, Shanto led his side to an unforgettable victory, proving his words right. Despite lingering inconsistencies in overseas conditions, Bangladesh's Test side is undeniably making quiet but significant strides forward.

The statistics highlight this dramatic transformation: in their first 20 years, Bangladesh managed only 14 victories from 119 matches. In contrast, over the past five and a half years, they have secured 13 wins from 41 Tests, with 12 victories in their last 24 matches over three and a half years, culminating in this historic win against Australia on home soil.

At the core of this turnaround is an unprecedented depth in the pace attack, moving away from a defensive reliance on home spin traps. This potent pace battery is now capable of dismantling opposition lineups abroad, arguably placing it among the top teams in world Test cricket, even without key players like Nahid Rana and Shoriful Islam.

Furthermore, Bangladesh's lower-middle order has become highly impactful, with positions 6 through 8 averaging over 35 runs per innings in recent wins. Batters like Mehidy Hasan Miraz and Litton Das have consistently formed crucial fifty-plus partnerships under pressure, while numbers 8 and 9 have contributed significantly to the team's total runs.

Despite these advancements, recurring top-order failures, lapses in batting temperament, and lingering inconsistency remain major areas of concern. Performance fluctuations in upcoming Tests would not be a surprise.

The structural shift away from heavy spin reliance began under Mominul Haque's captaincy, yielding immediate success with the landmark 2022 Test win against New Zealand. Shanto has since continued this tactical continuity, injecting fresh momentum and a modern flair.

While not yet an established Test power, Shanto and his team are moving in the right direction with a clear vision, leaving behind years of struggle. These recent statistics serve as strong testimony to their ongoing evolution.

headline: Master BCS viva competency questions with the global 'STAR' method: Your guide to success
summary: The Public Service Commission (PSC) is shifting to competency-based interviews, requiring candidates to demonstrate real-life problem-solving skills rather than memorized answers. The internationally recognized STAR method offers a structured approach to prese
details: The Public Service Commission (PSC) is adopting internationally recognized competency-based interview methods for BCS viva, moving away from traditional question patterns. This new approach requires candidates to prove their qualifications through real-world work examples, not hypothetical statements or memorized facts.

To address the challenge of presenting real-life stories accurately and concisely during a short viva, a globally used strategy called the 'STAR' method is highly effective. This method can be a game-changer for candidates in structuring their competency-based answers.

STAR is an acronym for four English words: Situation, Task, Action, and Result. It provides a four-step framework to organize and present any real-life event clearly and effectively to the interview board.

'Situation' involves briefly describing the context of when and where the event occurred. 'Task' identifies your main responsibility or challenge in that situation. 'Action' highlights the specific steps you personally took to handle the situation. 'Result' clearly expresses the positive outcome of your actions.

For example, when asked about solving a problem in an adverse situation, a candidate can use STAR. Imagine a national seminar where the main speaker fell ill 30 minutes before the event. The task was to secure an alternative speaker quickly and ensure the audience remained unaware of the disruption.

The candidate's action involved contacting a senior professor who was an expert in the field, persuading them to speak, and coordinating with the team to slightly delay the main discussion. The result was a successful seminar without any perceived disruption, preserving the event's quality through quick decision-making.
This new method renders traditional memorized advice and ready-made answers from coaching centers ineffective. Competency-based interviews cannot be taught through fixed notes or commercial courses.

Attempting to present memorized or fabricated stories from coaching centers will lead to failure under cross-questioning by experienced board members. Deep follow-up questions will expose any lack of genuine, personal experience.

The key to success in this method is to look inward at your own life experiences rather than memorizing handouts. Candidates should create a "diary" or notebook of their honest, real-life experiences.

Candidates are advised to list 10-12 true incidents from their university life, club activities, part-time jobs, event management, volunteer work, or social and family life. Each incident should then be structured into four to five lines using the STAR format.
